parts.spoken_English: Dolly was born at Roslin, Scotland, on 5 July 1996.
Her genome came from a Finn Dorset ewe's mammary cell, fused with a Blackface egg stripped of its nucleus.
A Blackface surrogate carried the embryo through pregnancy, yet her white face was proof of a genetically different lineage.
She alone survived from 277 attempts, an extraordinary failure rate.
Dolly is popularly called the first clone, a misconception.
Her predecessors included frogs cloned from transplanted nuclei in 1962 and Roslin's embryo-derived duo, Megan and Morag, in 1995.
She was genuinely the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.
Roslin's announcement on 22 February 1997 coincided with the paper, and her name, a mammary pun, honoured Dolly Parton.
The news provoked uproar and apprehension about the ethics of human cloning.
In March 1997 Clinton prohibited federal funding for such experiments.
In 1999 her telomeres, or chromosome tips, were reported shortened by about 20% for her age.
That fed anxiety; some speculated she was ageing prematurely.
Dolly was put down, aged six, on 14 February 2003, with arthritis and a progressive lung disease caused by a sheep virus.
In July 2016, 13 clones, four from her cell line, were ageing normally, without hypertension or diabetes.
In November 2017, her skeletal X-rays showed ordinary arthritis, and fears of early onset were judged unfounded.
She bore six lambs by natural mating; Bonnie, first of these descendants, arrived in April 1998.
Since 2003 her stuffed body, now famously an icon and memorial, has been encased in the National Museum of Scotland.
Behind glass, her white face plainly testifies to her Finn Dorset ancestry.
